summary: Tom and his brother built Avenue, a website widget that helps tradespeople, electricians and mechanics show services and take enquiries or bookings through their websites and Google. Tom says revenue reached AUD 85,000 per month, and describes using an existing marketing agency to fund the product and in-person sales to find early customers. The interview covers the product, its growth and technology costs, while Gus suggests applying similar tools to other local business niches. Tom’s main advice is to get customers to commit before building.

ideas.name: Avenue website widget for trades
ideas.one_liner: A website embed and Google booking flow that lets trade businesses show services and receive purchase requests or enquiries.
ideas.customer: Tradespeople, electricians and mechanics. The team initially approached a wide range of open businesses and found trade businesses responded best.
ideas.problem: Customers who want to buy from service businesses may have to call or email, and businesses can miss sales outside their opening hours.
ideas.offer: A branded website embed that presents services visually and guides customers toward a purchase or enquiry. It also connects with Google reservations and a Google My Business portfolio, and includes SMS as another part of the product.

pricing.notes: The transcript gives revenue and technology costs but no customer price.

acquisition_channels.details: The team visited open businesses without skipping types at first, demonstrated the product in person, initially on an iPhone and later on iPads, and used printed brochures. They explained that the widget could help businesses get sales outside their hours. Trade businesses responded better, and some unsuitable prospects referred them to other businesses.

quote.text: Door to door sales, essentially, like going and showing people our product, initially show it on an iPhone and then go, oh, what is it? It's like an app. No, it goes on to your website.
quote.speaker: Tom

acquisition_channels.details: Some businesses that did not need the product referred the team to friends whose businesses might benefit. The founders also say that being seen by many prospects helped them approach larger clients.

quote.text: However, you should speak to my friend because this would work so well for his business.
quote.speaker: Tom

ideas.delivery: Avenue is embedded on a client's website and displays its services in a visual format. A Google booking button leads to a client-branded form; users who exit are sent back to the client's website, where the widget is also embedded. Google and website contacts are brought to one place. Tom built it with his brother and a team that included a lead designer, a head developer and a front-end developer.

Tom described Stripe activity reaching almost AUD 63,000, but the period is not stated.
Tom named AWS, Slack, Google Workspace and Twilio costs; the transcript does not state their currency or billing period.
tools: Lusha (transcribed as “Last shot”; likely the lead-finding tool)
Claude (transcribed as “core”; likely the AI tool)
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. Tom says he used income from his existing agency to fund the start of Avenue and hired a team while the product had no revenue.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Tom says the project had zero revenue when he hired the team, but does not say when it first earned revenue.

acquisition.how: Their main described acquisition method required a person to visit businesses, demonstrate the product and handle feedback. Software could help identify prospects, but would not replace the in-person sales they described.

onboarding.how: A customer-facing form and website embed may make some setup repeatable, but the transcript does not explain how clients are onboarded or how website and Google integrations are configured.

delivery.how: The widget and booking flow can run as software after setup. The team built and maintained the product; the transcript does not say whether each client needs manual configuration or ongoing work.

billing.how: Tom showed revenue in Stripe, which can support automated payment processing, but the billing model and payment workflows are not described.

support.how: No customer support process is described. Human support may be needed for trade-specific service setup, website integrations or booking issues.

uk_applicability.notes: The product serves local service businesses and embeds on websites, so the basic model transfers to UK trades. Google availability and customer booking habits may need local setup. Any SMS marketing or messaging features should comply with UK PECR consent rules.

risks: Early prospects were confused about whether the product was an app or a website embed; the team changed the demonstration format and printed brochures.
Tom hired a team while Avenue had no revenue and describes this as a terrible idea that he does not recommend. The launch depended on cash from his previous agency.
In-person customer acquisition is labour-intensive and depends on a founder or salesperson making visits.
Tom says Twilio was a large part of the SMS costs; the transcript does not explain margins or how those costs scale.
For UK use, SMS and other electronic marketing must be designed around applicable consent requirements.

tactics.name: Use in-person demos to find and explain the product
steps: Visit open local businesses, initially without limiting outreach to one industry.
Show the product in person; the team began with an iPhone, then switched to iPads to make the website embed clearer.
Print brochures that explain what the product does.
Explain the customer benefit in concrete terms: the widget can help capture sales outside business hours.

quote.text: So we switched to iPads and then printed like brochures explaining what the product was.
quote.speaker: Tom

tactics.name: Use prospect responses to identify a better niche
steps: Show the offer to a range of businesses and observe which groups respond.
Ask for direct feedback, including from prospects who do not need the product.
Follow referrals to businesses the prospect believes are a better fit.
Adapt the product to suit the needs of the group that shows sustained interest.

quote.text: So trades kind of found us. We weren't looking, but they kind of kept being interested or kept showing kind of interest in the product.
quote.speaker: Tom

tactics.name: Sell before building
steps: Explain the customer problem and the solution before investing in a full product.
State the price and ask whether the prospect is willing to commit or hand over the money.
Treat a real commitment as evidence that the idea may be worth building.

quote.text: If you can get someone to commit before building a product, you've probably found something worth this showing.
quote.speaker: Tom

tactics.name: Build an MVP, then add specialist roles
steps: Ask a developer friend to help create an MVP that tests whether the embed can work on a client's website.
After the layout begins to work, bring in design and development specialists to improve the interface and build the backend and frontend.
Tom's team included a lead designer, a head developer and a front-end developer.

quote.text: February lost year. I had a friend that was a developer and he helped like create like the MVP basically to see that it could be done
quote.speaker: Tom

tactics.name: Use the existing business to fund the new product
steps: Tom used income from his marketing agency and website-hosting clients to fund Avenue.
The agency continued operating with limited attention while he worked to transition into Avenue.

quote.text: So I used my like very precious income that I did have to live to basically fund the start of this and try and transition out of the agency into this full time.
quote.speaker: Tom

lessons.lesson: Get a prospective customer to commit at a stated price before building the full product.

quote.text: If you can get someone to commit before building a product, you've probably found something worth this showing.
quote.speaker: Tom

lessons.lesson: A simple product can work when it solves a real problem for a specific customer.

quote.text: You just need to spot a real problem and solve it
quote.speaker: Gus

lessons.lesson: Direct conversations can reveal which customer group has the clearest need, even if the founder did not initially target that group.

quote.text: So trades kind of found us. We weren't looking, but they kind of kept being interested or kept showing kind of interest in the product.
quote.speaker: Tom

lessons.lesson: Treat rejection and direct criticism as useful product feedback, and use referrals to find a better-fit customer.

quote.text: But if you really do love your product, that's the feedback you're actually looking for.
quote.speaker: Tom

lessons.lesson: In-person selling can help explain a product that is difficult to understand from a description alone and can build familiarity with larger prospects.

quote.text: But we didn't have any connections to get into those bigger clients if we didn't do the hard work of getting this follow on first.
quote.speaker: Tom

lessons.lesson: Make the product's value concrete by explaining what it helps the customer do, such as capturing sales outside opening hours.

quote.text: when you show someone the problem they have and you can explain it quite clearly like, you can't get sales outside of ours. This fixes that.
quote.speaker: Tom

lessons.lesson: An existing business can provide cash to fund a new venture, but this can make the new venture dependent on the old business's income.

quote.text: So I used my like very precious income that I did have to live to basically fund the start of this
quote.speaker: Tom

lessons.lesson: A founder does not need coding experience to start a software venture if they can bring together the people needed to build and test it.

quote.text: I didn't have any coding experience. I'd never kind of design anything myself, but I knew what it would take to kind of put the team together
quote.speaker: Tom

lessons.lesson: Software can appeal because it may keep earning after the initial work, but finding a real customer problem still takes iteration.

quote.text: you can still be making money while you're sleeping, even if you've already done the work.
quote.speaker: Tom

evidence_quality.rationale: Tom is a first-hand founder and shares specific product workflows, acquisition tactics, team roles and revenue figures. The transcript includes unclear auto-captioned wording, incomplete cost context, and revenue figures in different currencies that are not reconciled.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Gus includes a HubSpot partner promotion for a free database of business ideas; it is an in-video promotional segment.
